home.description: Helix is a free, GNOME-compatible desktop for Linux. Your apps keep working, your settings come with you, and you can switch back to GNOME from the login screen any time.

hero.tag: In everyday use as a main desktop
hero.title: A fresh desktop for Linux, {highlight}
hero.subtitle: Helix is a GNOME-compatible alternative desktop: your apps work as they are, your settings come with you, and you can switch back from the login screen any time.
hero.imageAlt: The Helix notification list beside a calendar: grouped chat notifications, a mail and a software update notice, today's events, a world clock and media controls.
hero.imageCaption: Notifications, your calendar, world clocks and media controls, side by side.
hero.agents: New: Agent Access, so AI agents and command-line tools can work with your desktop under your control.

why.title: Try something new without starting over
why.lead: “GNOME-compatible” means Helix works with the same apps and settings as the GNOME desktop that Ubuntu and many other Linux systems use. It looks and feels like its own desktop, but your computer stays yours.

apps.title: Your apps just work
apps.text: GNOME apps, web browsers like Chrome and Chromium, Electron and Qt apps and older X11 programs all run as they are. Nothing to reinstall.

settings.title: Your settings come with you
settings.text: Your wallpaper, dark style, fonts, keyboard layouts, shortcuts and accessibility settings are shared with GNOME, so Helix feels like your computer from the first login.

switchBack.title: Switch back any time
switchBack.text: Helix installs next to GNOME rather than replacing it. Pick whichever desktop you want each time you log in, and change your mind whenever you like.

install.title: Install Helix in three steps
install.lead: Helix has ready-made packages for Ubuntu and Debian, Fedora and Arch Linux, for regular PCs and for ARM computers (Arch: PCs only), from its own package repository. It sits next to your current desktop and doesn’t replace it.

install.title: Install
install.text: Install {full}. It brings in {desktop}, the apps ({apps}) and everything else Helix needs.
install.updates: From now on, Helix updates along with the rest of your system.
install.manual: Prefer not to add a repository? Download the packages from the {desktopReleases} and {appsReleases} instead; the {guide} has the details.

login.title: Log out and pick Helix
login.text: At the login screen, choose {helix} from the session menu (on Ubuntu, it’s the gear button that appears after you pick your name) and log in.

reassure.text: To switch back, log out and pick it again at the login screen. Your settings are shared, so nothing gets lost either way.

greeter.summary: For enthusiasts: use Helix’s own login screen
greeter.intro: Optional, and for Ubuntu and Debian only for now. Install {package} from the Helix repository (it brings in greetd), then switch login screens and restart:
greeter.switchLabel: Commands to switch to the Helix login screen
greeter.back: To switch back, or if the login screen doesn’t appear (press Ctrl+Alt+F3 for a text login first):
greeter.backLabel: Commands to switch back to GDM
greeter.settings: Once it’s in use, Settings has a Login Screen panel for its options: the user list, a banner, the accent colour and the clock format.

nvidia.title: Have an NVIDIA graphics card?
nvidia.text: Helix needs the NVIDIA driver’s modesetting option turned on ({option}). You only need to set it once.

help.title: Need a hand?
help.text: The full guide covers every step, and you can ask a question or report a problem on GitHub.

repo.title: Add the Helix repository
repo.text: Pick your package manager, then run these commands once in a terminal. They add the repository’s signing key and the repository itself, so your system can install Helix and keep it up to date.
repo.commandLabel: Commands to add the Helix repository with {manager}
repo.pacmanNote: The fingerprint is the repository’s signing key; check that it matches the one shown at packages.dakr.io/helix before you trust it.

tour.title: A complete desktop for every day
tour.lead: Helix isn’t a demo. It’s a full desktop that people use every day, with everything you’d expect to find.

topBar.title: Top bar and quick settings
topBar.text: Volume, brightness, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, power modes, night light and dark style, one click away.

notifications.title: Notifications and calendar
notifications.text: Your notifications next to a calendar with your events, world clocks, the weather and controls for whatever is playing.

overview.title: Overview and workspaces
overview.text: See all your open windows at a glance and spread your work across workspaces that appear as you need them.

appGrid.title: App grid and dock
appGrid.text: Find every app in the grid, sort them into folders, and pin favourites to a dock that’s there from the start.

screenshots.title: Screenshots and recording
screenshots.text: Take a screenshot or record a video of your screen, built right in.

lock.title: Lock and login screens
lock.text: A lock screen with media controls and notification summaries, and, if you want it, Helix’s own login screen, with its options in Settings.

tour.quickSettingsAlt: Helix quick settings: volume and brightness sliders, toggles for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, airplane mode, night light, dark style and do not disturb, power modes, and lock, suspend, log out, restart and power off.
tour.quickSettingsCaption: Quick settings, in a teal accent colour.
tour.loginAlt: The Helix login screen: a clock and date, a user's initials and name, a password field, Restart and Power Off buttons, and a session menu set to Helix.
tour.loginCaption: Helix’s own login screen, here with a blue accent.

fileChooser.title: Open and save dialogs
fileChooser.text: One file chooser for every app, in Helix’s look: places, a list or a grid of thumbnails, and the same settings as GTK’s own.

languages.title: In 12 languages
languages.text: The desktop, lock and login screens come in Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Russian, Chinese, Japanese and more, with right-to-left layouts mirrored.

extensions.title: Extensions of its own
extensions.text: Add panel items, quick settings toggles and dock items. Each extension runs as its own program, and can run in a sandbox.

apps.title: Comes with its own apps
apps.text: Helix installs with a set of everyday apps made for it: a file manager, a terminal, a text editor, settings, a web browser and more. The GNOME apps you already have work just as well.

access.title: Accessible, and made to fit you
access.intro: Helix is built to be usable by everyone, the way you like it.
access.keyboard: Full keyboard control of the top bar, quick settings, notifications, menus and dialogs
access.contrast: High contrast, larger text and reduced motion
access.keyboardAndZoom: An on-screen keyboard and a magnifier
access.accent: Follows your accent colour and dark style, on the desktop and in your apps
access.note: A few parts of the desktop don’t work with screen readers or larger text yet. We track those openly and are working through them.

differences.title: Familiar where it matters, thoughtful in the details
differences.lead: Trying Helix doesn’t lock you in: GNOME stays on your computer and you can move between the two from the login screen. Here’s what to expect.

safeChoices.title: Safe choices by default.
safeChoices.text: When a dialog pops up, pressing Enter picks the safe option, like Cancel or Deny, and keys pressed the instant it appears are ignored, so you can’t approve something by accident.

extensions.title: Extensions can’t crash your desktop.
extensions.text: Each extension runs on its own, so a broken one can’t take the rest of the desktop down with it.

logout.title: Logging out just works.
logout.text: An app that has crashed can’t hold up logging out forever.

look.title: A look of its own.
look.text: The top bar, overview and lock screen are Helix’s own design, with easy-to-read text and visible keyboard focus. Your apps look just as they do now.

shellExtensions.title: GNOME Shell extensions don’t run.
shellExtensions.text: Helix has its own extensions instead. Your GNOME extensions stay installed for when you go back to GNOME.

notACopy.title: It doesn’t look exactly like GNOME.
notACopy.text: Helix works with GNOME’s apps and settings, but it isn’t a copy of GNOME’s desktop.

young.title: It’s young software.
young.text: Its translations into 12 languages are machine translations still awaiting review, and some hardware, like touchscreens and drawing tablets, hasn’t been tried on real devices yet.

differences.link: See what works and what doesn’t

hardened.title: Hardened where it counts.
hardened.text: Thumbnails are made in a sandbox, the desktop’s private interfaces check who is calling, and links and downloads from untrusted places ask before they open.

how.title: How Helix works
how.text: Helix is an independent desktop, built in Rust for reliability. It isn’t a fork of GNOME: it speaks the same public interfaces that GNOME’s apps and tools rely on, and every one of them is written down in an open specification. The docs tell the whole story.

source.title: Free and open, for everyone
source.text: Helix, its apps and its specification are dedicated to the public domain (CC0): free to use, share and change, with no strings attached. Follow along, report a problem or help out.
source.desktop: The desktop itself, and its login screen.
source.apps: Files, Terminal, Text Editor, Settings, Web and more.
source.spec: The open specification behind the docs.

agents.title: Let AI agents help, on your terms
agents.lead: Agent Access lets coding assistants, scripts and other agents read your desktop and act on it through the {command} command. The desktop itself enforces what they may do, and it stays off until you turn it on.

levels.title: Four levels, you choose the most.
levels.text: Read only, Control the desktop, Control apps, and Screen and input. Each agent gets no more than you approve in a prompt that only you, at the computer, can answer.

indicator.title: Always visible, always stoppable.
indicator.text: While an agent is at work, the top bar shows it, with Stop. Touch the keyboard or pointer and an agent’s typing and clicking stops at once.

never.title: Some things are never exposed.
never.text: The lock screen, password fields, system password prompts and Settings are off limits, and so is any app you exclude.

log.title: A log of what it did.
log.text: Every request is recorded, refused ones too, without the text or secrets involved. Read it in Settings or with {command}.

agents.terminalCaption: With access at the Control the desktop level:

meta.title: Agent Access
meta.description: Agent Access lets AI agents and command-line tools read and act on your Helix desktop through helix-agent, with access levels, consent prompts, an indicator with Stop, exclusions and an activity log you control.

hero.title: AI agents on your desktop, {highlight}
hero.subtitle: Coding assistants, scripts and other agents can read your Helix session and act on it through the {command} command. The desktop decides what they may do, asks you before any agent gets access, and shows you when one is at work.
hero.offNote: Off by default. Turn it on in {path}.

principles.title: How it stays in your hands

shell.title: The desktop enforces it
shell.text: The shell checks every request itself. {command} is a thin client with no rules of its own, so a program that talks to the shell directly meets exactly the same checks.

consent.title: You approve each agent
consent.text: The first time an agent asks, a prompt names it and the access it wants: Deny, Allow for this session, or Always allow. Agents can’t answer it, neither over D-Bus nor with synthetic input. Deny has the focus, and keys and clicks in its first second are ignored.

off.title: Off until you turn it on
off.text: Nothing is allowed until you switch Agent Access on. Turning it off ends every agent’s access at once.

noSelfGrant.title: No way to grant itself access
noSelfGrant.text: No request lets an agent give itself access, and changing settings grants nothing by itself. Sandboxed apps (Flatpak, Snap) are refused outright.

levels.title: Four levels, each including the one before
levels.lead: You set the most any agent may have, and each agent gets no more than you approved in its prompt. Lowering the level narrows every agent at once; raising it widens none.

readOnly.name: Read only
readOnly.text: See windows, apps, workspaces, monitors, notifications and recent files, search files and wait for windows. Ask you a question, ask for a yes or no, or set you a reminder.

desktop.name: Control the desktop
desktop.text: Also launch apps, open files and links, manage windows and workspaces, switch quick settings, set volume and brightness, and show notifications labelled with the agent’s name.

apps.name: Control apps
apps.text: Also read and use apps’ buttons, fields and menus through the accessibility tree, the way a screen reader does.

screen.name: Screen and input
screen.text: Also take screenshots and send keys, text, clicks and scrolling into one window. Settings offers this level on its own, behind a warning.

notifications.name: Notifications
notifications.text: Agents may read notification titles and bodies. Without it they see only which app sent one, and when.

clipboard.name: Clipboard
clipboard.text: Agents may read and set the clipboard. Even then, what Settings, system prompts and excluded apps copied, and password managers’ secrets, stay out of reach.

textFields.name: Read text fields
textFields.text: Agents that control apps may read what is typed in apps’ text fields.

confirm.name: Confirm sensitive actions
confirm.text: You confirm each sensitive action before it happens: closing a window, switching Wi-Fi or airplane mode, and anything an agent marks as sending, deleting or paying.

remote.name: Remote sessions
remote.text: Agents running in a remote login (SSH) are refused unless you allow them.

watch.title: You can always see it, and stop it

indicator.title: An indicator in the top bar
indicator.text: While an agent is active, the top bar shows an indicator, like the one for screen sharing. It can’t be turned off. Its menu lists each active agent and its level, and says so when an agent is taking screenshots or sending input.

stop.title: Stop, for each agent
stop.text: Stop ends that agent’s access straight away. Even an agent you always allow is suspended for the rest of the session: its next request asks you again.

hardStop.title: Your input wins
hardStop.text: Press a key, click, move the pointer, scroll or touch the screen, and an agent’s typing and clicking stops at once, even in the middle of a word. New input from agents is refused for the next two seconds.

locked.title: Nothing while locked
locked.text: While the screen is locked, agents can do nothing at all, and a consent prompt that was showing goes away unanswered.

never.title: What agents never get
never.lead: These aren’t settings, and they can’t be turned off.
never.lockScreen: The lock screen and the login screen.
never.passwords: Password fields: their contents are never read, and agents can’t set them or type into them.
never.prompts: System prompts: while a password, keyring, network, Bluetooth pairing or consent prompt is open, agents can’t read apps, take screenshots, send input or use the clipboard.
never.settings: The Settings app, so no agent can reach the Agent Access page.
never.excluded: Apps you exclude: their windows are left out of every list, they can’t be launched or controlled, and they appear black in screenshots.
never.screenshots: Screenshots are drawn by the compositor, with the desktop’s dialogs, notifications and protected windows blacked out. The pointer is never drawn.

settings.title: One page for all of it
settings.text: {path} holds the main switch, the access level, whether agents are asked every session or may be remembered, the switches above and your excluded apps. It lists the agents you allowed, by their real program, with Revoke, Forget and Revoke All, and the reminders agents have set for you.

log.title: An activity log you can read
log.text: The shell records every agent request, refused ones included, and your answers to its prompts. Open it with View Activity in Settings, or run {command}.
log.private: The log never holds what agents typed or read: no text, clipboard contents, notification text, window titles, field values or search queries, and for a link only its scheme and host.
log.retention: Entries stay in your own files for 30 days by default (anything from 1 to 365), and you can clear them from Settings.

cli.title: One command for agents
cli.lead: {command} prints readable text on a terminal and JSON when its output is piped, with its own exit code for every kind of refusal, so an agent can tell when it needs you. It comes with a man page and completions for bash, zsh and fish.
cli.name: Set {variable} to show your agent’s name in prompts, the indicator and the log. The name is for display only: agents are told apart by their program.
cli.refusal: When access is off, the answer says so, and where to change it:
cli.refusalLabel: The JSON answer when Agent Access is off

isolation.title: It isn’t a sandbox.
isolation.text: A program you run unconfined can already change your files and settings. Agent Access governs what agents do through the desktop, and makes sure no request can get access without you.

sensitive.title: The desktop can’t tell what a click does.
sensitive.text: Agents should mark sending, deleting and paying as sensitive so you’re asked first; closing windows and switching Wi-Fi or airplane mode always count.

x11.title: Password fields need the app’s help.
x11.text: Typing into a password field is blocked when the app reports it, as GTK, Qt, Firefox and Chromium do; older X11 apps can’t be checked.

docs.title: The full details
docs.lead: Agent Access is specified in the open, like everything else in Helix.
